newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-SAfrica Sept reserves seen slightly.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-SAfrica Sept reserves seen slightly.

text.p: South Africa's gold and foreign exchange reserves are expected to have fallen slightly in September as importer demand offset the effects of offshore buying of local bonds and equities.

According to a Reuters poll of 10 economists, gross reserves would come in at 10.06 billion rand in September from 10.08 billion in August. The average forecast was drawn from a range of 9.8 billion rand to 10.5 billion rand.

Peter Worthington, emerging markets economist at J.P. Morgan in London, echoed most economists' sentiments when he said portfolio flows were likely to have been offset by importer demand for dollars during the month.

Johannesburg Stock Exchange figures show foreigners were net buyers of 453.16 million rand worth of equities in September, while Bond Exchange data shows foreigners purchased 68.56 million rand worth of gilts during the month.

"If you looked at portfolio flows they were positive in the month, but then towards the end of the month there was importer demand for dollars...those two factors probably offset each other," Worthington said.
Another economist also noted that while the average exchange rate and money market shortage improved in September from August, month-end data showed a weakening in the two.
"That indicates there was some improvement in the month but that they (reserves) came under pressure at the end of the month," she said.
Econometrix economist Tony Twine said he expected a slight improvement in the reserves amid signs that capital imports were beginning to slow.

"We are beginning to detect some slowdown in the rate of capital imports and if the squeeze from the current account is beginning to diminish, the reserves could chalk up a positive move...but it is not going to be very big," Twine said.
The gold component of reserves could also have declined slightly as a result of a lower rand gold price.
The Reserve Bank said its gold holdings would be valued at 1,550.46 rand per ounce in September compared with 1,567.26 in August.
One economist said it was unlikely that the central bank had bought back any of the gold reserves it has sold off in recent months, which would result in a lower gold valuation.
Since May, the Bank's gold reserves have declined from 4.66 million ounces to 3.99 million ounces in August.
The reserves data is scheduled for release on Monday at 1600 GMT but officials said on Friday morning it was possible that the figures could be released later today.
Also due for release next week is August producer inflation data. Economists forecast an average 7.2 percent year-on-year rise and a 0.9 month-on-month increase.
The average was drawn from a 7.1 to 7.5 percent range.
Economists said the main contributor to a rise in the year-on-year rate would be a low base. PPI rose just 0.3 percent month-on-month in August last year and 7.8 percent year-on-year.
The imported component of the index, which has confounded economists expectations in recent months after the rand's depreciation since February 15, was also expected to play a part.

"I think we will see quite a bit of pressure from the import side. The rand was weaker in both July and August...and the rand oil price was also significantly higher in both July and August," one economist said, adding that rising food prices would also play their part.

Another economist added, however, that a 13.7 percent decrease in base metal prices since May -- when the prices were last surveyed by the Central Statistical Service -- was likely to subdue the monthly increase.
August PPI will be released at 0900 GMT on Tuesday.
